title: Love the messenger: genuine passion from the person sells better than a polished message
summary: Jason Cohen uses a Korean restaurant waiter's broken-English answer ("Dolsot bibimbap better!") to argue that the messenger matters more than the message once a human relationship begins. Websites need specificity, but in sales, support and tradeshow conversations, genuine passion, knowledge and a desire to make the customer successful is what sells.

principles.text: Obsessive, genuine excitement is contagious and is itself good sales, in any industry and for any product.
principles.quote: Being obsessively and genuinely excited about something is contagious. And good sales. In any industry, with any product.

principles.text: In a live human interaction, who delivers the message matters more than the polish of the message.
principles.quote: It's the messenger, not the message, that made the experience wonderful.

principles.text: Be specific on websites, because websites are attention-getters and information-distributors, not relationships.
principles.quote: So yes, on websites you do need to be specific because websites aren't relationships; they're attention-getters and information-distributers.

principles.text: Once the human relationship starts (sales pitch, tech support, tradeshow booth), lead with genuine passion, knowledge and a desire to make customers successful.
principles.quote: But as soon as the human relationship begins--whether by sales pitch or tech support or tradeshow booth--the most important thing is to be genuine in your passion, knowledge, and desire to make your customers successful.

principles.text: A sincere recommendation from someone who cares beats a mechanically recited pitch, and can steer a customer to the higher-value choice.
principles.quote: It was perfect because it wasn't in an ad, wasn't in a datasheet, wasn't part of a 30-second elevator pitch mechanically regurgitated on a tradeshow floor.
